subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Asian Disease Problem
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Asian Disease Problem usable.

hook.text: 600 people will die. Plan one saves 200 for sure. Plan two: 33% chance of saving all 600. Most choose certainty.

buildup.text: Now reframe: Program C means 400 die for sure. Program D: 33% chance nobody dies. Most pick D. Same math.

discovery.text: The 'save' frame triggers risk aversion. The 'die' frame triggers risk seeking. Words alone flip the preference.

twist.text: Kahneman and Tversky showed this to doctors, policymakers, and statisticians. Everyone was susceptible.

climax.text: Before deciding, reframe the problem both ways. If your preference reverses, you're being framed, not informed.

punchline.text: Same facts, different frames, opposite choices.

quiz.question: What did the Asian Disease experiment demonstrate?
options: People always choose the safest option
Framing as gains or losses reverses risk preferences
Only non-experts are affected by framing

details.summary: Kahneman and Tversky's Asian Disease Problem showed that when a treatment is framed as saving 200 of 600 people, most choose it. When the same treatment is framed as 400 people dying, most prefer a risky gamble. The outcomes are identical.
details.whyItMatters: This experiment became the most famous demonstration of framing effects in decision making. It proved that preferences are not stable and rational but are constructed in the moment based on how information is presented.
takeaways: Identical outcomes produce opposite preferences when framed differently
Gain framing produces risk aversion; loss framing produces risk seeking
This experiment is the cornerstone demonstration of prospect theory

faq.question: What exactly is the Asian Disease Problem?
faq.answer: Participants choose between programs to combat a disease affecting 600 people. Program A saves 200 for certain. Program B has a one-third chance of saving all 600. When framed as lives saved, people choose A. When reframed as deaths, they choose B.

faq.question: Has the Asian Disease experiment been replicated?
faq.answer: Yes, extensively across cultures, professions, and contexts. The framing effect is robust. Even medical professionals and policy experts show the same reversal, demonstrating that expertise does not eliminate susceptibility to framing.
